findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves, so they can say what the site is about before scrolling.
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The title and heading are about firstmate, a different project, so a newcomer arriving at Athena's home page may first think the site is about firstmate. Only the lede shows that this page is a demonstration of what Athena can do.
The page explains why the firstmate study is here: it is evidence of what Athena can do. That makes the long body easier to follow once the reader knows its purpose.
findings.source: "A study is Athena's written reading of another software project, taken at one fixed commit... to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it"

findings.text: The next steps are concrete and in order: prerequisites, clone, install, then a first command with a description of what happens. The header links straight to this section, so the reader knows what to do next.
findings.source: Next steps: "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm" ... "./setup.sh" ... "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The lede does not say which models Athena uses, what it typically costs, or what a commit with its trace looks like. A newcomer deciding whether to try it has to go to the repository for that.
findings.source: Header lede: "has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost"

findings.text: This header link is meant for the project owner and is not explained. A newcomer cannot tell whether it is meant for them.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: Almost all of the page is dense detail about firstmate's internals (exit codes, places-held, pending-close records). That shows how carefully Athena traces its sources, but it is more than a newcomer to Athena needs. The lede and next steps are the only parts written for that reader.
findings.source: Headings "States of a piece of work", "Transitions", "Glossary", "Claims and sources"

findings.text: This refers to the repository's internal layout without saying which repository or why it matters to the reader. It helps a contributor but not a newcomer.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"
